title: AI in Manufacturing: Preserving Institutional Knowledge
summary: As veteran engineers retire, manufacturers are using AI agents to capture institutional knowledge. See how Wolfspeed and United Rentals do it with Snowflake.
body_markdown:
## *AI Isn't Replacing Manufacturing's Domain Experts — It's Making Sure Their Expertise Outlasts Their Tenure*


Think about who actually keeps your plant running: Not the ERP system. Not the maintenance manual binder. It's the process engineer who has spent 15 years learning this specific press, this specific line and these specific failure signatures. The maintenance technician who knows from the sound of a conveyor whether it needs a bearing or a motor. The shift supervisor who knows, from years of hands-on experience, the precise machine tweaks needed to keep every product batch running smoothly.


That expertise — specific to your facility, accumulated over years — is the invisible infrastructure behind your operational performance. And it exists almost entirely in human heads, not in any system you own.


Manufacturing is now confronting the consequences of that reality. As experienced operators and engineers approach retirement, companies that haven't begun capturing that expertise face a version of the data fragmentation problem, but one that’s harder to solve: Once the knowledge walks out the door, you can't recover it from a legacy historian or a spreadsheet backup.


The “Global AI & Data Trends Survey,” which gathered responses from 2,050 enterprise leaders including 288 in manufacturing, reveals a workforce undergoing active transformation — and points to a window that is closing faster than most executives realize.


### The myth that AI is eliminating manufacturing's experts


The narrative that AI is replacing experienced workers in manufacturing doesn't hold up against the data. Job losses among senior individual contributors in manufacturing are running at 33%, compared to 41% across all industries surveyed. Manufacturing is protecting its domain experts at a higher rate than the cross-industry average.


What's actually changing is the distribution of work. The same survey shows that 62% of the job displacement occurring in manufacturing is concentrated at the entry level — roles that handle a large amount of rote, repetitive data manipulation and manual operational tasks. AI isn't erasing expertise; it's automating the work that never required it.


This distinction matters deeply to how you think about knowledge preservation. Your most experienced engineers are not at risk of being replaced by an algorithm. Rather, they’re at risk of retiring before your organization has preserved what they know.


### The knowledge capture imperative


Wolfspeed operates 24/7 automated cleanroom fabs where every minute of unplanned downtime is a direct margin hit. When a complex assembly tool fails, the difference between a fast resolution and an extended outage often depends on whether the right engineer is available and whether they can recall, under pressure, the precise sequence of steps that worked the last time this specific failure mode appeared.


To address this, Wolfspeed built a custom AI agent on Snowflake — feeding it raw chat history from engineering conversations, maintenance logs and operational data accumulated over years of plant operation. The company built not just a faster troubleshooting tool but a permanent record of how Wolfspeed's best engineers think through complex tool failures.


Despite that, Wolfspeed's leadership is clear-eyed about a risk that comes with this approach: AI models can confidently misinterpret operational context, especially in highly plant-specific environments. So the company established a mandatory framework for trusted autonomy. The first principle is that data can’t just be clean; it must carry the explicit institutional context of the specific plant's operational processes. Building a semantic layer isn't just a technical data-cleanup task — it's the process of translating years of shop-floor experience into rules the AI can follow. The second principle is that all automated troubleshooting guides must natively incorporate audited plant safety procedures, because under production stress, technicians will follow AI instructions. That compliance can’t depend on whoever built the agent having a good day.


So now, when a new technician joins a Wolfspeed facility, the AI agent can draw on the documented troubleshooting history of the plant's most experienced engineers, with guidance built around the plant’s audited safety procedures.


### The skills bridge in action


United Rentals, managing 1,650 highly decentralized branches and 49,000 telematics-enabled assets, faces this problem at scale. Field technicians encounter a constant stream of equipment fault codes across dozens of makes, models and production years. The knowledge required to resolve those codes efficiently lives with master mechanics who have seen them before. But experienced mechanics aren't always available, and incoming technical talent is expected to perform at the same level from the start.


The company deployed its Business Intelligence Agent with Snowflake to bridge that gap. Instead of requiring technicians to manually search through thousands of pages of equipment manuals, the tool instantly links a fault code to the exact page and section needed to execute a fix — encoding the lookup expertise of experienced mechanics into a system anyone on the team can use from Day 1.


Within 30 days of rollout, 4,000 field personnel were active users. An industrial workforce that had historically resisted digital tools adopted this one almost immediately, because it didn't ask them to change how they work; it just made them better at the work they were already doing.


This is the model for institutional knowledge transfer at scale: not documentation projects or training programs, but AI systems that make expert judgment accessible at the moment of need.


### The workforce transformation already underway


The survey data reveals something that doesn’t always surface in the AI-in-manufacturing conversation: A resounding 77% of organizations surveyed have experienced active job creation due to AI. Among companies experiencing both job creation and displacement simultaneously, more than two-thirds confirm the net employment impact has been positive.


What's emerging is a new tier of AI-native manufacturing roles that didn't exist five years ago. Supply chain prompt engineers who move fluently between physical operations and digital systems. Digital twin analysts who drive autonomous production optimization and predictive maintenance at scale. AgentOps engineers who keep multiagent systems running reliably in production environments.


The practical difference is significant. A master scheduler operating in a pre-AI environment might spend the first three hours of a shift manually tracing a shipment delay across five disconnected systems, running manual calculations to adjust the week's production schedule and making calls to the floor to adjust the lines. The same person reskilled into an AI-augmented role audits an agentic supply chain system that has already detected the delay, run a predictive capacity simulation and surfaced options, all before their first cup of morning coffee. By midmorning, the disruption is resolved and the worker's attention shifts to the high-value work AI can’t do: supplier negotiations, escalation judgment and relationship management.


The true ROI of AI lies not in how many workers you can cut, but in how fast you can turn your existing workforce into an elite layer of AI supervisors.


### The cost of waiting


Manufacturers who treat AI purely as a head count reduction lever rather than a knowledge preservation and workforce elevation opportunity face a compounding risk. The veteran operators and engineers who drive operational performance will migrate to competitors where their expertise is augmented, not constrained by manual bureaucracy. And recruiting the next generation — workers who expect to orchestrate agentic systems rather than push buttons in legacy platforms — becomes significantly harder in organizations that haven't built that infrastructure.


The institutional knowledge your plant runs on exists right now, in the heads of your most experienced people. Capturing that knowledge now with the power of agentic AI will make all the difference between whether it’s still accessible five years from now or whether it retires along with the people who carry it.
